candidate.answerReason: After extending outcomes to five games, exactly five equally likely sequences satisfy B winning game two and A winning the series. Exactly one also has B winning game one, so the probability is 1/5, agreeing with choice A.

methods.label: Complete every series to five games
methods.explanation:
Imagine recording five independent fair game outcomes, continuing with imaginary games if the series has already ended. This preserves the series winner: whichever team first reaches three wins necessarily has at least three of the five recorded wins. Thus A wins the series exactly when A wins at least three of the five games.

Game two is a B win, so A must win three or four of the remaining four positions. There are four ways for A to win exactly three: choose the one remaining position won by B. There is one way for A to win all four. These give five distinct sequences satisfying the given information.

Independence and fairness make all five-game sequences equally likely, so these five admitted sequences are equally likely. If B also wins game one, A must win games three, four, and five. Exactly one of the five sequences has this form. Therefore the requested probability is \(\boxed{\frac15}\), choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses a finite equally likely outcome space and small direct counts, making the conditional probability accessible without a named inversion formula.

methods.label: Weight the actual series
methods.explanation:
Write each actual series as a string of game winners, stopping when a team reaches three wins. We must account for series of different lengths having different probabilities.

Since B wins game two, A cannot finish the series in three games. If A finishes in four games, the only possible history is \(ABAA\). If A finishes in five games, the final game is an A win and the first four games contain two A wins and two B wins. With game two fixed as B, the other B win is in position one, three, or four. The three histories are
\[
BBAAA,\qquad ABBAA,\qquad ABABA.
\]
These disjoint cases exhaust all histories satisfying the given information.

By independence, the four-game history has probability \((\frac12)^4=\frac1{16}\), and each five-game history has probability \((\frac12)^5=\frac1{32}\). Only \(BBAAA\) has B winning game one. Hence the requested conditional probability is
\[
\frac{1/32}{1/16+3/32}=\boxed{\frac15},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{A}\).
methods.levelReason: Uses exhaustive short histories, multiplication for independent outcomes, and addition of disjoint probabilities.

candidate.annotationRationale: Conditional probability is the route-neutral target, and independence supports both methods. The first method constructs equally likely fixed-length completions and counts the restricted outcomes. The second retains the actual stopping rule and sums unequal history weights. Combination formulas, total-probability formulas, and Bayes' formula are not prerequisites for these written methods.

review.mathematicalCheck: The completed five-game model has five equally likely outcomes satisfying the information, with only BBAAA also satisfying a first-game B win. Independently, the stopped histories have total probability \(1/16+3/32=5/32\), with favorable probability \(1/32\); both give \(1/5\), choice A.
review.levelCheck: Both methods explain their sample spaces and probability weights using elementary counting and independence.
review.methodDistinctness: Equally likely completions and weighted stopped histories offer distinct, useful ways to handle the stopping rule.
review.annotationCheck: Conditional probability is route-neutral, independence supports both methods, and the counting and probability operations remain method-local.
